parts.title: Heads and Tails: What Cats' Ears and Tails Tell Us About How Cats, Felis catus, Signal to Each Other
parts.abstract:
Simple Summary

Animals of the same species need to communicate with each other, so they can decide how close to get and how far to stay. Part of this communication is made of visual signals, which can be simple or complicated. We wanted to work out which features matter most in a particular kind of visual signal: the way a cat holds its tail and its ears at the same time when it meets another cat. People often notice a cat's tail, but we show that when two cats meet, the position of their ears is the best clue to how the meeting will turn out. When cats meet people, though, the cat most often came up to a person with its tail held up, before rubbing itself against the person. These results help us better understand how cats see people, and they will help people look after cats' well-being.

Abstract

Animals communicate with their eyes, using particular signals. One kind of signal is the position of body parts that can move, such as the ears or the tail. We studied these combinations of ear and tail positions in cats. Our goal was to find out which features of these combinations mattered most when cats met other cats, and when cats met people.

We watched 29 cats for a total of 100 hours. We started watching whenever a cat walked towards another cat, a method called "Behavior dependent onset of sampling". We then recorded every interaction we saw, a method called "All occurences" sampling. Altogether we recorded 254 meetings between two cats, plus 10 meetings between a cat and a person.

In each cat–cat meeting, we noted the ear and tail positions of both cats, and how the meeting ended. It ended positively or neutrally, or negatively. In most of the 254 meetings, both cats held their tails down. Ear position, on the other hand, was a key clue to how a meeting would end. When both cats held their ears upright, the meeting was significantly positive, for example with rubbing or the cats staying close together. In every other ear combination, the meeting was negative, and the cats moved further apart.

The tail did not seem to play an important part in how cats signal to each other. But holding the tail up mattered when a cat came up to a person. In the great majority of these cases, the cat rubbed itself against the person's leg or legs. We may therefore conclude that a person has a special meaning in a cat's world, probably because cats and people have lived together for a very long time. Pet owners need to understand the signals cats use with other cats and with people, so that they can help cats live well.
parts.introduction_first:
When animals interact, they communicate. As the scientist Marler [1] pointed out, communication helps animals of any species decide how close to get and how far to stay. This matters most in social species, such as most primates.

In a meeting between two animals, one animal, the sender, sends signals to the other, the receiver, through one or more channels, such as sight or sound. The receiver reads these signals. But the receiver also takes into account who the sender is, and the situation around them. An observer can tell things about the sender, such as its sex or size. However, there is no reliable way to know which clues from the situation the receiver actually used. Menzel and Johnson [2] compared the situation to a "garbage pail": it holds a huge amount of different information, so we cannot tell exactly which of it the receiver pays attention to.
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

We showed that when two cats meet, the ear positions of both cats, whether they match or differ, are a good clue to how the meeting will end. Cats seemed to pay more attention to the head and face, which are also part of the visual signal that includes the position of the tail.

Studying the visual signals of pets such as cats matters in two ways. First, it helps us better understand how cats communicate. Second, what scientists learn should be used to teach people, so that it helps protect the bond between cats and people and helps cats live well.
parts.introduction_rest:
In every species, signals have been shaped over the course of evolution by several different processes. The scientist Tinbergen [3] described these processes and grouped them under the idea of "ritualization". One process is "emancipation": a signal breaks away from the body function it first came from. Another is "stereotypy": a signal becomes more fixed, so it varies less from one time to the next.

Visual signals are controlled by particular patterns of movement that involve body parts that can move. Scientists often call these visual signals "displays". A display is any visual pattern that other animals of the same species can see and that might change how they behave. In reality, displays are complicated patterns made of many signals at once [4].

In this paper we use the word "configurations" for a different kind of visual pattern. A configuration is a combination of postures and of the positions of body parts that can move, such as the ears, the tail or the mouth. A display looks at the whole picture at once. A configuration, by contrast, can be thought of as a set of clearly separate movements of different body parts, including the head. This means we can study particular configurations by looking at each of their parts.

Configurations match the reference frames that Golani [5] suggested for describing the movements animals use when they interact. A reference frame is a way of describing movement by choosing what it is measured against. Golani proposed two kinds. The "bodywise" reference frame is about the animal itself. The "partnerwise" reference frame is about the other animal in the pair. In the bodywise frame, the different moving parts of one animal's body (the head, mouth, ears, neck, back and so on) can move in relation to each other. In the partnerwise frame, we look at where the two animals in a pair stand in relation to each other. To describe an interaction, we therefore need to use both frames at the same time.

In some mammal species, the tail is an important part of the bodywise frame. Very often, scientists study the position of the tail and the facial expressions separately. However, all these movements should be seen together, as making particular configurations within the bodywise frame.

This raises a question. Suppose one cat comes up to another with a certain facial expression and its tail between its legs. Does that mean the same thing as when the cat comes up to its partner with the same facial expression but its tail held up? If we study facial expressions without the tail, or the tail without the facial expressions, we cannot answer this question.

The problem of how complicated emotional signals are does not stop with signals that use only one channel, such as the visual ones we have just described. It also applies to signals that use two channels, especially signals that combine sight and sound. In general, scientists study calls and other sounds in great detail, but separately from the postures or facial expressions that go with them. The sender's demeanor, meaning its overall attitude, is often mentioned, but it is not studied together with the sounds, as in [6].

Partan and Marler [7] looked at the question of signals that use several channels. They asked whether a signal from one channel meant the same thing when it was sent alone as when it was sent together with a signal from another channel. Baraud and colleagues [8] showed that when calls were combined with different postures or other visual behaviors, the calls did not simply repeat what the visual signal already said. Instead, they added extra information that seemed to make the visual signal alone less likely to be misunderstood.

As for visual signals, Kiley-Worthington [9] studied many mammal species to find out what the position of the tail might do during interactions, alongside other patterns of movement. She suggested that the way animals use the tail in displays is linked to its main job, which is helping them move. So, in her view, tail movements in displays have not broken away from what first caused them [9].

Studies of real animals have given mixed results. In baboons, Hausfater [10] showed that a neutral tail position was linked to social rank in females, but not in males. Hausfater also found no difference between the sexes in how they used tail position. On top of that, the neutral tail position of top-ranking males and females was no different from that of other baboons. Hausfater [10] therefore concluded that in baboons, the way the tail is held is not a signal linked to changes in social rank, but simply a change in body shape.

Schenkel [11] described different tail positions in wolves and gave each one a mood, but only based on his own personal impressions. Also, whatever its position relative to the body, the tail can be still or waving, with different sizes of wave and different speeds. In wolves, Harrington and Asa [12] showed that the position of the base of the tail was linked to social rank. This idea has been confirmed in dogs [13]. However, more experiments are needed to find out what part tails play in communication.

Sounds can be studied in great detail and split into a number of separate features. These include pitch (how high or low a sound is), how the pitch changes, loudness, and structure, such as whether a sound has a clear tone or not. Visual displays, on the other hand, are rarely broken down into their parts. One important exception might be the Facial Action Coding System, proposed by Ekman [14] to study facial expressions in humans. This system has been adapted for several species and for different purposes, for example for chimpanzees [15] and for macaques, in a version called MaqFACS [16]. It has been used especially to judge pain, in horses [17] and in laboratory mice [18,19]. The position of the ears, as part of configurations that include facial expressions, is an important visual signal in some domestic animals, such as dogs [20] and horses [21].

Cats are usually thought of as a solitary species, although cats may gather in groups around food [22,23,24,25]. As a species, cats are neither social nor solitary. How well cats put up with each other varies a great deal, which is unusual for a solitary species (for example, [26]). Darwin [27] gave a lively, detailed description of cats in different situations, showing that they express different emotions. His description covered the cat's general posture, the position of the ears, how wide the mouth opens, the position of the tail, and the many different ways the tail can move.

Configurations in cats could very easily be drawn from these descriptions. Later, Leyhausen [23] drew the main facial expressions of cats along two imagined scales of motivation: aggression and fear. Leyhausen's drawings show what we mean here by "visual configurations". The parts of a cat's facial configuration include, in particular, movements of the ears, opening of the eyes and opening of the mouth, which usually go together with making sounds ([23], p. 195). Since this first work, several studies have supported some of Leyhausen's facial expressions, especially by using the idea of the Facial Action Coding System for cats, called CatFACS, to study different sides of cat behavior in experiments [28,29,30,31]. Bennett and colleagues [28] used CatFACS together with a cluster analysis, a method that sorts things into groups that are alike. With this, they gave experimental, number-based support to some of the facial expressions that Leyhausen [23] first described. Their experiments let them link particular emotions precisely to particular facial expressions.

Along the same scales of aggression and flight, Leyhausen [23] also drew body configurations. These include how the body is held in relation to the ground, the line of the back, and the position of the tail ([23], p. 194). Bradshaw and Cameron-Beaumont described ear positions in cats [32] (p. 73). It is worth noting that the figure shows more than ear positions. It actually shows what we call a "visual configuration", because the posture, the head and neck, the mouth and the eyes are clearly shown separately.

Bradshaw and Cameron-Beaumont [32] studied what they called the "Tail up display", a particular upright position of the tail that cats take during interactions. They looked at whether the cats involved, the sender, the receiver or both, held their tails up. Cafazzo and Natoli [33] studied the use of the tail-up display in a colony of cats in Rome. They found that the tail-up display was a friendly signal. It was also more common in females. It was also more often followed by rubbing than by nose sniffing. They reported that low-ranking cats showed the tail-up display more often than high-ranking cats. They also reported that the cats' ranking, based on how much aggression they gave and how much they received, was closely linked to age. So, according to their analysis, the oldest cats were the most aggressive towards the youngest ones. The youngest cats, when coming up to an older cat, held their tail up, probably to hold back the aggression they expected from earlier encounters.

In all these studies, the position of the ears or the position of the tail was studied separately (see also [34]). In addition, Cameron-Beaumont [35] studied the tail position of the sender and that of the receiver separately.

However, during interactions, animals keep exchanging signals and making sense of information in a way that Tinbergen [4] called a "chain of reactions". He showed this with the zig-zag dance that sticklebacks, a kind of fish, use to court [36]. Because interactions work this way, one might argue that the signals of the sender and the receiver were not independent of each other. Nor were they independent of the other parts of the whole visual signal.

In this study, we set out to study "visual holistic configurations", meaning whole visual signals, instead of looking at their parts separately. Our aim was to work out which parts of these visual configurations matter most when cats interact. We focused on the position of the ears and the position of the tail. We also compared these visual configurations when cats met other cats and when cats met people.
parts.methods:
2. Where the Cats Lived, Who We Studied, and How We Did It

2.1. Where the Cats Lived and Who We Studied

We carried out this study in a cat shelter called AVA, in Cuy Saint Fiacre, France. AVA is short for "Aide aux vieux Animaux", which means "Help to Old Animals". The shelter took in cats that had gone missing, pet cats that had been abandoned, and pet cats that their owners had left behind. The cats lived in an enclosure of about 2600 square meters.

The enclosure had grass, trees, bushes and shrubs. It also had litter boxes and other suitable places where cats could go to the toilet, fallen trees and other spots where they could scratch, and boxes that could hold one or two cats. There were also bungalows, which are small cat houses (Figure 1). The bungalows could be heated and had shelves, beds and blankets, and they could hold a score of cats. Cats could find places to eat and drink at different spots near the bungalows.

2.1.1. A Note on Ethics

AVA means "Aide aux vieux Animaux" ("Help to Old Animals"). This tells us that the cats living at the shelter are meant to be adopted as pets. If a cat is not adopted after it arrives, it will spend the rest of its life at the shelter. Trained staff, including two vets, look after the cats. None of the cats we studied carried FIV or FeLV, two viruses that can cause serious illness in cats. The AVA Association, which runs the shelter, follows French rules. Our study was observational and non-invasive, which means we only watched the cats and did not handle or change anything about them. The shelter's Director approved it.

2.1.2. The Cats We Studied

About 50 cats lived in the 2600 m2 enclosure. Because the cats could move around freely, each one could easily choose how far to be from the others. Some cats wanted to be close and in contact, while others wanted to keep their distance.

Before we started recording, we gave the cats time to get used to being watched. During this time, one of us (EJ) picked out twenty-nine cats from the 40 to 50 cats living there. We recognized each cat by its coat color and pattern, and by other clues when needed. We chose the 29 cats that were the easiest to see at any time in the enclosure. Because the cats were meant to be adopted, the number of cats might change over time.

All the cats we picked out stayed in the enclosure for the whole study. Since the cats could roam freely, the staff did not handle them as a routine. The staff came into the enclosure twice a day to feed the cats and clean the bungalows and boxes. Cats might hide somewhere in the enclosure, so the staff only dealt with cats that came up to them. No cat was ever forced to be handled.

The cats we picked out included 13 males and 5 females. For 11 cats, we could not tell whether they were male or female. All of them were cross-breed cats, meaning they were not purebreds. Eleven had been neutered, four were intact (not neutered), and for 14 we did not know. The staff told us each cat's sex and whether it had been neutered.

The cats in the enclosure were moderately attracted to people, even though they were used to them. So the observer being in the enclosure did not change how the cats behaved, and it did not stop cats from meeting each other.

2.2. How We Did It

2.2.1. Watching the Cats

We watched the cats during two periods, one in winter and one in summer. The winter period was three weeks of 5 days each in February, and the summer period was two weeks of 5 days each in early September 2006. We watched at 4 different times of day (8 h, 12 h, 14 h and 18 h), for 1 hour each time. Altogether, we watched for 100 hours.

Before we started, we drew a map of the enclosure showing everything in it (Figure 1). On the map, we divided the enclosure into imaginary squares, each 20 m by 20 m, wherever the shape of the enclosure allowed (Figure 1). These squares helped us say exactly where each cat was, both in which square it was in and in relation to particular structures or objects in the enclosure.

During each watching session, the observer (EJ) moved to different places in the enclosure, one after another, until she had seen the whole enclosure. The order of these spots changed at random from one session to the next and from one day to the next. At each spot, the observer looked around and then started recording using "Behavior dependent onset of sampling" [37]. In this method, recording begins when a particular behavior happens. Here, that behavior was a cat walking towards another cat, with its head and body turned towards the other cat. To count as one cat coming up to another, the two cats had to start no more than 3 m apart. We call the cat that walked towards the other the "Initiator", and the other cat the "Receiver".

We also recorded cats coming up to people, but we only looked at the behavior of the cat. When a cat came up to a person during a session, the person had to stand still and was told not to respond to the cat. We left out any cases where a person came up to a cat.

During the meetings, we used "All occurrences" sampling [37], which means we recorded every meeting we saw. At each watching spot, the observer stayed still, at a distance from the cats that ranged from less than one meter to several meters. The observer never interacted with the cats. We only included meetings, between cats or between a cat and a person, that involved cats we had recognized.

We stopped recording a meeting as soon as both cats moved away from each other, or as soon as only one cat moved away, or as long as both stayed in contact or close together. We called a meeting "negative" whenever it could be seen as aggressive, with fighting or threatening behavior, or with one cat running away or avoiding the other. We called a meeting "positive-friendly" or "neutral" when the two cats stayed in contact, sniffed each other's noses, rubbed against each other or licked each other, sat or lay close together, or when one cat simply walked past. So how a meeting ended depended on how the distance between the two cats changed. At first, the distance shrank as one cat came up to the other (see [1]).

We wrote down every meeting by hand. In total, we recorded 254 meetings between two cats that we had recognized, plus 104 meetings between a cat and a person.

2.2.2. What We Recorded

At the start of each meeting, we noted the position of the tail and the position of the ears for both the Initiator and the Receiver. We looked at the tail and the ears of both cats at the same time.

We called these combinations of ear and tail positions "visual configurations". They are based mainly on the "bodywise" system described by Golani [5], which describes body positions in terms of the body itself. We used three kinds of ear position: "erect" (see positions A0B0 and A1B0 [23] (p. 195), and "forward and erect" [32] (p. 73) and [28]), "flattened" against the sides of the head (see positions A0B1 and A1B2 [23] (p. 195), "flat" [32], and see [28]), and "moved down and backwards" (see position A0B2 [23] (p. 195), "back and flat" [32], and see [28,34]). We also used two kinds of tail position: "Up", as defined in Cameron-Beaumont's study [35], and whether the tail was held level or below the line of the cat's back. In both kinds of tail position, we did not take into account how the tail was moving.

2.2.3. How We Turned the Observations into Codes

Our goal was to record the ear and tail positions of both cats at the same time. For each ear position, there could be two different tail positions: "up" or "not up" (Figure 2). For each cat, we then wrote a 4-digit code. The first digit was for the tail: 1 for "Up" and 0 for "Not up". The next three digits were for the ears: 1 for the position we saw and 0 for each of the other two positions (Figure 2).

We also gave each coded meeting an ending: "positive/neutral" or "negative". We used the same coding for meetings between a cat and a person, but only for the cat. So in that case, the meeting was coded only by a 4-digit number.

2.3. How We Analyzed the Data

To analyze our data, we used a statistical test called the G-test. It checks whether the numbers we counted fit a pattern we would expect by chance, such as an even spread, or whether two things are linked. We used it on contingency tables, which are tables that count how often each combination of categories turns up. Here, the tables had one row and one column, with R rows and C columns [38]. We compared the G values we got with Chi2 values for particular degrees of freedom, which are numbers that depend on how big the table is.

We also used the Chi2 test and the binomial test, which is a test for yes-or-no outcomes. Depending on whether we were comparing separate groups or looking at a single group, we used these tests either to check whether counts fit an expected pattern or to analyze contingency tables [38,39]. We also used a test to check whether two percentages were equal [40].

All our tests were "two-tailed", which means they looked for differences in either direction, higher or lower. We set the cut-off for statistical significance at p = 0.05. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference or link, a result this large would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. The Ear and Tail Combinations We Saw When Cats Met Other Cats

To see which combinations of ear and tail positions turned up, we built a large table with 6 rows and 6 columns. Each row shows the sender's combination, and each column shows the receiver's combination. Each square in the table shows how many times that pair of combinations appeared. The squares along the diagonal are the cases where both cats held the same combination.

There are 36 possible combinations of tail and ear positions, but we actually saw fewer than half of them: 16, or 44.4% of the 36 (Figure 3). In 77.6% of the meetings (197 out of 254), the cat that came up to the other cat held its tail down (Figure 3).

In 75.6% of the meetings (192 out of 254), both cats held their tails down. Only in 2.4% of the meetings (6 out of 254) did both cats hold their tails up, whatever their ears were doing (Figure 3). The sender held its tail up while coming up to the other cat in 22.4% of the meetings (57 out of 254), whatever the receiver's tail and ears were doing.

To check whether two things are linked, we used a statistical test called a G-test of association. It asks whether two things, here the sender's combination and the receiver's combination, tend to appear together more often than chance alone would predict. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For p < 0.05, that means less than 5% of the time.

Because so many combinations were rare, we could not run this test on all the combinations we saw, even when we grouped some rows and/or columns together. So we looked at just one case: the sender coming up with its tail up and its ears upright (code 1100). The receiver's combinations in these meetings were not spread evenly across the table (first row of the table; G = 81.4, df = 5, p < 0.001; Figure 3). The receiver held its tail down and its ears upright significantly more often than expected (Chi2 = 79.6, df = 1, p < 0.001; Figure 3).

There was also a trend for both cats to hold the same combination. This happened in 45.3% of the cases we saw, but only 6 of the 36 possible combinations (16.7%; Figure 3). Since both cats held their tails down in most meetings, it is likely that the position of the ears carries most of the information about how the cats feel. So we then made a smaller table with 3 rows and 3 columns, showing the sender's ear position as the rows and the receiver's ear position as the columns (Figure 4).

The ear position of the sender and the ear position of the receiver were significantly linked (G = 27.8, df = 2, p < 0.001; Figure 4). When the sender did not hold its ears upright, both cats held their ears in the same position significantly more often than expected (Figure 4).

3.2. Ear and Tail Combinations at the Start of a Meeting, and How the Meeting Ended

We were able to judge how 196 meetings ended. Some combinations were rare, so we had to group some of them together to get enough cases. In the end, we studied only four combinations of tail and ear positions, and only one of these had the sender holding its tail up. We then built a table with 4 rows and 2 columns. Each row is one of the four combinations of the sender's and receiver's tail and ear positions, and each column is one of two possible endings: positive or negative (Figure 5).

Some combinations were significantly linked to how the meeting ended (G-test, G = 52.14, df = 3, p < 0.001). When both cats held their ears upright and the receiver held its tail down, the ending was positive significantly more often, no matter which way the sender held its tail (Chi2 = 5, df = 1, p < 0.05 in both cases, Figure 5). The opposite happened when the sender held its tail down and its ears upright, and the receiver also held its tail down but its ears were not upright. In that case, the ending was negative significantly more often, whether the receiver's ears were flattened or held backwards (Chi2 = 14.6, df = 1 for flattened ears and Chi2 = 10.2, df = 1 for backwards ears; both p < 0.0001; Figure 5).

Next, we wanted to look only at the ears, whatever the tail position of either cat. So we built another table with 4 rows and 2 columns. The four rows were: one, both cats with ears upright (100100); two, the sender with ears upright and the receiver with ears not upright (ears flattened and ears backwards, 100010 plus 100001); three, the sender with ears not upright and the receiver with ears upright (010100 plus 001100); and four, both cats with ears not upright (010010 plus 010001 plus 001010 plus 001001).

Because some groups had very few cases, we had to merge the last two rows. This gave us a table with 3 rows and 2 columns. The three rows were: both cats with ears upright; the sender with ears upright and the receiver with ears not upright; and both cats with ears not upright. The two columns were again positive and negative endings (Figure 6).

Of the 196 meetings we judged, about half ended positively (43.9%) and the rest negatively (56.1%). The ear positions of both cats were significantly linked to how the meeting ended (G = 80.55, df = 2, p < 0.001; Figure 6). When both cats held their ears upright, the meeting was significantly likely to end positively (Chi2 = 22.1, df = 1, p < 0.0001; Figure 6). The cats then stayed in contact for a long time, rubbed against each other, licked each other, or stayed close together.

When the two cats held their ears in different positions, or when neither cat held its ears upright, negative endings were significantly more likely than expected. This was true when one cat had its ears upright and the other not (Chi2 = 6.8, df = 1), and when neither cat had its ears upright (Chi2 = 8.4, df = 1; both p < 0.01; Figure 6). Most negative endings happened when one of the cats, especially the receiver, or both cats had their ears not upright. This was the case in 80.9% of the negative meetings (Figure 6).

3.3. Tail Position When Cats Came Up to Other Cats and to People

In the great majority of meetings between cats and people, the cat came up to the person with its tail up and its ears upright (code 1100 plus code 1001, 97.8%). When a cat came up with its tail down, it always held its ears not upright, either flattened or backwards.

We compared the tail positions of the cats in the 257 cat–cat meetings and the 104 cat–human meetings, using a table with 2 rows and 2 columns (Figure 7).

Tail position was significantly linked to the type of meeting (G = 115.7, df = 1, p < 0.0001; Figure 7). Cats held their tails up significantly more often than expected in meetings with people (Chi2 = 43.5, df = 1, p < 0.001; Figure 7). Cats also held their tails up more often in meetings with people than in meetings with other cats (t = 11.27, df = ∞, p < 0.001; Figure 7).
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

We had 29 cats, so there were 406 possible pairs of cats that could have met. Only 126 of these pairs actually met. This shows that cats are not social animals, but they can live in groups when they choose to [22,23,24,33,41]. This unusual way of life, together with the fact that cats of the same species can put up with a lot of each other, may be why the domestic cat, Felis catus, is such an expressive species.

In this study, we combined the visual signals described by Leyhausen [23], looking at the ears and the tail together. We did this whether or not the cat's mouth was open. An open mouth is usually linked with making sounds, so we would have called these "multimodal configurations", meaning signals that use more than one channel. We showed that, in meetings between two cats, the position of the ears was the feature that mattered most in shaping how the meeting went.

Kiley-Worthington [9] wrote that a cat's tail position is more about the cat's general body tension than about communication. We did not look at the many different and complicated ways a cat's tail can move.

Our results only partly support what Cameron-Beaumont said: that holding the tail up is a friendly signal [33,35]. She looked only at the position of the tail, ignoring other visual signals such as the position of the ears [35]. She also studied the cat that started the meeting and the cat that received it separately, for each meeting [35]. Cafazzo and Natoli [33] also looked only at the tail. They showed that cats held their tails up more often when they were the ones receiving the most aggression. These cats were also the youngest in the group. Only one cat was a young cat, and it was the only cat in the colony that had not been neutered or spayed. Cafazzo and Natoli [33] suggested that holding the tail up was a friendly signal, one that stops aggression.

Kiley-Worthington [9] was writing about how tail positions might be used for communication. Even so, she mentioned that both the ears and the tail matter for communication in cats. We call this the "tail–ears configuration". Our study of these combinations shows clearly that, when two cats meet, the position of the ears matters more than the position of the tail, for both cats.

It is worth noting that Leyhausen showed only one tail-up position among the 16 combinations he described for meetings between cats [23]. Ear position is an important visual signal. It is part of the face in cats, and also in other domestic animals such as dogs and horses. Because cats meet face to face, it is not surprising that the relative positions of their ears can predict how a meeting will end. Ear positions probably show a range of feelings, from friendly to defensive to threatening, along the three main kinds of behaviour in a meeting: friendliness, defence and threat [23].

Many mammals have strong muscles that let them move their ears [42]. Scientists have studied ear positions in some domestic animals, such as horses [21], sheep [43] and dogs [20], to find out how much these positions communicate or how they show feelings in general. In these animals, ear position has been shown to matter more than tail position, even though a raised tail is easy to see. Unlike what was seen in sheep [43], in cats, as in dogs and horses, the two cats in a pair moved their ears in matching ways. Only when both cats held their ears upright did this point to a positive feeling, and the meeting ended positively.

4.1. What This Means for Cats' Well-Being

We showed that the visual signals cats use when they meet other cats are very different from the ones they use when they come up to people. In meetings between cats, the position of the ears seemed to be the most important feature. When cats came up to people, though, they usually used only one visual signal, with the tail held up. Correia-Caeiro and colleagues [44], who studied how dogs and people interact, made an important point: what matters to one species might not matter as much to another, especially when the two species are only distantly related.

Ekman's FACS [14] is a system for describing the tiny movements of the face. It inspired recent research that looked at very fine details of the "visual face configuration", meaning the way a cat's face is arranged [28,30,31]. These experiments aimed to spot signs of pain or stress in cats. For cats' well-being, this is extremely important. However, it seems unlikely that cats, when they meet other cats, were picking up some or all of the fine details of the face that these studies revealed.

As for the position of the tail, Cafazzo and Natoli [33] suggested that cats in charge made lower-ranking cats come up to them with their tails held up. If we apply this idea to cats coming up to people, we might guess that cats see people as being in charge of them. However, the idea of a ranking, or hierarchy, has been criticised, both in social species such as primates [45] and in meetings between dogs and people [26,46]. When rankings are built on aggression, they are often linked to other things, such as sex, weight or age [33,47].

Instead of seeing people as being in charge, we suggest that cats see people as their carers. Seen this way, the way cats come up to people is similar to the way kittens come up to and greet their mothers before they start to suckle. People know very well that a cat coming up with its tail held up is friendly, because this is usually followed by rubbing. People also know about other baby-like behaviours that cats show towards them: purring, kneading (pushing their paws in and out as if kneading dough), suckling, gently rolling onto their back, and even suckling (see [48]).

A cat coming up with its tail held up and its ears not upright may mean something different from a cat coming up with its ears upright. Being aware of this might be one way to understand cats' signals better. Over the course of evolution, the most noticeable features of how animals show their feelings have been shaped, through different processes, to be as clear as possible and to trigger particular responses (see [4]). This is true for meetings between animals of the same species. In meetings between different species, each species has to adapt to the signals the other species uses. People in particular may learn what their pets' signals mean through associative learning, which means learning by linking a signal with what happens afterwards [44].

People can easily see and understand where a cat's ears and tail are. Cats have been bred by people less than dogs have [49]. In dogs, this breeding has produced a huge variety of body types. As Bradshaw and Nott [50] pointed out, drooping ears and tails that have been cut short greatly change how well dogs can communicate, because these dogs look more like wolves. So a large number of cat breeds keep their ears and tails fully developed and easy to see, and this keeps their important ability to express themselves.

People can also learn in other ways, especially when they are around domestic animals. For example, they can look at the whole picture instead of focusing on just one feature, even if that feature is easy to see. (For examples of signals that use two channels, see [51].)

4.2. Limitations of Our Study

Our study focused on one question about how cats communicate, but many more things about how cats live in groups could have been studied. We did not use video recordings. This should certainly have been done, as long as this study was not only one part of a larger study of cats living in a group with a lot of freedom to move around.

All the cats were identified, so the different combinations of ear and tail positions could have been sorted out pair by pair, and the effects of sex and age could possibly have been explored. Our twenty-nine adult cats included a certain number of males and females. So the visual signals could have been studied separately for male–male, female–female and female–male meetings, to learn more about what these signals do. However, meetings were rare, and only 28% of all possible pairs of cats actually met. So we should have collected much more data.
